questions.q: Why can a script with no error handling be more dangerous than doing the same work by hand?
options: It doesn't notice a failed step and often just prints an error message while continuing on to later steps anyway
Scripts without error handling always run slower than manual work
PowerShell refuses to execute any script without a try/catch block
Manual console work never has any failures to compare against
questions.explain: Unlike a person who stops when they see an error, a script without error handling can keep executing later steps after an earlier one has already failed.

questions.q: What happens when code inside a PowerShell try block throws a terminating error?
options: Control jumps straight to the catch block, where the script can log the error and decide how to respond
The script immediately deletes all resources it created
PowerShell ignores the error and continues the try block from where it left off
The computer restarts automatically
questions.explain: try/catch lets the script detect the failure and respond deliberately, instead of leaving the outcome to chance.

questions.q: In the lesson's three-step provisioning example, what's the real risk if step 3 runs after step 2 has already failed?
options: Step 3 might run against a resource that was never created, either failing confusingly or silently succeeding against the wrong resource
Step 3 will always automatically retry step 2 first
There is no risk, because PowerShell validates every step before running the next one by default
Step 3 will simply be skipped without any consequence
questions.explain: Letting step 3 proceed after step 2 fails risks configuring something against a half-built or nonexistent resource, which can be confusing to debug later.

questions.q: What does calling exit 1 inside a catch block accomplish?
options: It stops the script and returns a non-zero exit code that a pipeline or scheduler can detect as a failure
It restarts the script from the beginning
It silently suppresses the error so the script can continue
It sets the exit code to zero, signaling success
questions.explain: A non-zero exit code is how automated systems like pipelines and schedulers recognize that a script failed.

questions.q: What is the practical recommendation this lesson makes for structuring a multi-step automation script?
options: Wrap each meaningful step in its own try/catch, and let catch stop the script rather than allow execution to continue past it
Put the entire script in one single try/catch block regardless of how many steps it has
Never use try/catch, since PowerShell handles all errors automatically
Only use try/catch for the very last step in a script
questions.explain: Wrapping each step individually and failing fast keeps a problem from cascading into later steps that depend on it.
